name: Infectious Complications of Bites
system: Skin and Soft Tissue / Infectious Disease

clinicalPearls: Bite-wound flora generally mirrors the oropharyngeal flora of the biting animal, though organisms from soil, the victim's and animal's skin, and animal feces may also contribute (p.1142).
Dogs account for about 80% of animal bites; roughly 15-20% of dog bites become infected, whereas more than half of cat bites and scratches become infected (p.1142-1143).

Cat bites carry a higher infection risk than dog bites because narrow sharp canine teeth inoculate deeply, predisposing to septic arthritis and osteomyelitis, especially with punctures over or near a joint of the hand (p.1143).

Dog-bite infection typically appears 8-24 h after injury with pain and cellulitis plus purulent, sometimes foul-smelling discharge; the bite-to-symptom interval is notably shorter for cat bites (p.1143).
Pasteurella multocida, a small gram-negative coccobacillus from feline oral flora, causes the majority of cat-bite infections and tends to advance rapidly, sometimes within hours (p.1143).

Capnocytophaga canimorsus following dog bites (or licking of open wounds) can cause fulminant sepsis, DIC, and renal failure, particularly in asplenic, immunosuppressed, or hepatically impaired hosts; this thin gram-negative rod is hard to grow on solid media and may need up to 14 days to grow on blood culture (p.1143).

Human bites become infected more often than other animal bites (~10-15%); clenched-fist ('fight bite') injuries are especially serious because deep hand structures including bone, joint, and tendon are inoculated (p.1144).
Eikenella corrodens is a fastidious organism particularly associated with clenched-fist injuries; the microbiology laboratory should be alerted when it is suspected (p.1144).

Rat-bite fever (Streptobacillus moniliformis in the US; Spirillum minor 'sodoku' mainly in Asia) characteristically manifests after the initial wound has healed; streptobacillary disease causes fever, migratory arthralgias, and a maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles (p.1143).
Aquatic exposures matter: alligator or piranha bites may harbor Aeromonas hydrophila, while shark, moray eel, and barracuda bites are associated with marine Vibrio species (p.1143).
Old World monkey (Macaca) bites can transmit B virus (Macacine herpesvirus 1), a cause of serious CNS infection; nonhuman primate bites otherwise resemble human bites (p.1143).
Seal, walrus, and polar bear bites can cause 'seal finger,' a chronic suppurative infection attributed to Mycoplasma species such as M. phocacerebrale (p.1143).
harrison.pathophysiology: Bite injuries inoculate the victim's tissues with the biting animal's oral flora plus environmental and cutaneous organisms, producing a typically polymicrobial mix of aerobes and anaerobes. Deep puncture wounds (cat canines, clenched-fist injuries) drive organisms into joints, tendons, and bone, predisposing to septic arthritis and osteomyelitis. Local spread produces cellulitis with purulent discharge, while seeding can lead to systemic disease (bacteremia, meningitis, brain abscess, endocarditis). Impaired lymphatic drainage (e.g., post-mastectomy limb) or immunocompromise (glucocorticoids, SLE, leukemia, cirrhosis, splenectomy) facilitates dissemination, and Capnocytophaga can incite DIC and renal failure in such hosts (p.1142-1144).
additionalDifferentials: Rat-bite fever versus Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Lyme disease, leptospirosis, and secondary syphilis (p.1143)
Localized bite-wound cellulitis versus tissue damage from snake envenomation, which can mimic infection (p.1145)
Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) as a late consequence of cat bites/scratches (p.1143)
infectionMimics: Inflammatory tissue necrosis from venomous snake envenomation, which can be difficult to distinguish from secondary infection (p.1145)
nonInfectiousMimics: Traumatic soft-tissue injury, crush injury, and laceration without infection
additionalInvestigations: Gram's stain and aerobic culture of all infected wounds; anaerobic cultures when abscess, devitalized tissue, or foul-smelling exudate is present (p.1144)
Notify the microbiology laboratory when fastidious organisms such as Eikenella corrodens are suspected in human bites (p.1144)
White blood cell count, and blood cultures if systemic infection is suspected (p.1144)
Radiographs of penetrating wounds to assess fracture or retained foreign body such as a tooth fragment (p.1144)
Hand-surgery consultation for hand injuries to evaluate tendon, nerve, and muscular involvement (p.1144)
For suspected Capnocytophaga sepsis, prolonged blood-culture incubation (up to 14 days); organisms may be seen within polymorphonuclear leukocytes on Wright-stained peripheral smears (p.1143)
redFlags: Asplenia, hepatic dysfunction, or immunosuppression after a dog bite raising concern for fulminant Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis with DIC and renal failure (p.1143)
Clenched-fist ('fight bite') injury over the metacarpophalangeal joints with possible joint, tendon, or bone involvement (p.1144)
Systemic features: fever, lymphangitis, lymphadenopathy, or signs of bacteremia, meningitis, or endocarditis (p.1143)
Rapidly advancing inflammation within hours suggesting Pasteurella infection (p.1143)
Suspicious human-bite wounds prompting evaluation for domestic or child abuse (p.1144)
Bites posing rabies risk, requiring contact with public-health authorities (p.1144)
harrison.prognosis: Most localized bite-wound infections resolve with appropriate wound care and treatment, but a significant minority become severe or life-threatening. Septic arthritis and osteomyelitis prolong the course. Capnocytophaga sepsis can be fulminant in susceptible hosts. Streptobacillary rat-bite fever was frequently fatal in the preantibiotic era and may be complicated by endocarditis, myocarditis, meningitis, pneumonia, and multi-organ abscesses (p.1142-1145).
pitfalls: Underestimating infection risk in cat bites, whose deep punctures seed joints and bone despite small surface wounds (p.1143)
Missing occult joint/tendon involvement in clenched-fist injuries because patients often present only after frank infection develops (p.1144)
Failing to consider rat-bite fever when illness appears after the original wound has already healed (p.1143)
Inadequate anaerobic culture when devitalized tissue or foul-smelling exudate is present (p.1144)
Not alerting the lab to fastidious organisms (e.g., Eikenella, Capnocytophaga) that require special or prolonged culture conditions (p.1143-1144)
Primary closure of high-risk wounds (e.g., cat puncture wounds, wounds >12 h old on a limb or >24 h old on the face), which raises infection risk (p.1144)
harrison.severityClassification: Human-bite wound infection risk stratifies by depth: approximately 2% for superficial wounds versus over 25% for deep wounds such as clenched-fist injuries. Human bites are categorized as occlusional injuries (from actual biting) or clenched-fist ('fight bite') injuries (fist striking teeth), the latter being more common and more serious owing to inoculation of deep hand structures (p.1144).
